article.title: AI delivers ‘zero financial payoff’ to most companies, Apollo economist says
article.summary:
In BriefAI hasn’t benefited the bottom line of any big corporations outside the tech industry, according to a note recently published by the chief economist at Apollo Global Management (the private equity giant that used to own TechCrunch).
Apollo’s Torsten Slok focuses on what he calls the S&P 493 — the S&P 500, minus Alphabet, Amazon, Apple, Meta, Microsoft, Nvidia, and Tesla — finding that profit margins and revenue per worker appear to be flat, with no evidence that AI is improving productivity.
“Despite massive investments and widespread hype around artificial intelligence, the technology has delivered zero financial payoff to corporate America outside of tech,” Slok said.
Is this simply a matter of non-tech companies lagging behind the tech giants?
Slok sounded skeptical, arguing that it will be tough for corporate America to “turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue growth and higher profit margins.”“AI may be a great calculator, but in business, intelligence is mostly judgment,” he wrote, later adding, “AI does not understand accountability, trust, culture, unwritten rules, ethical trade-offs or fairness, all of which shape reputational risk and ultimately drive revenue growth and profit margins.”Recent studies have also found that AI has yet to deliver significant productivity gains.

article.title: Not Wind, Not Solar: Japan's Renewable Project Makes Energy From Saltwater
article.summary:
Wind and solar power are both well established sources of renewable energy, but for nations with plenty of coastline, a promising emerging technology called osmotic power offers another possibility.
Osmotic power involves generating electricity from the natural interaction between saltwater and freshwater, and Japan has turned the intriguing idea into a working power plant.
The technology uses a membrane that separates saltwater from freshwater.
The membrane allows water molecules to pass through from the freshwater side into the saltwater side, while blocking most of the salt.
Japan, a country that's no stranger to exploring new energy technologies, began operating the osmotic power facility in the western city of Fukuoka in 2025 using concentrated brine left over from seawater desalination alongside treated wastewater.

“We don’t think there is a need to include 12-hour, 24-hour or 48-hour PM2.5 forecasts as having too many indicators may complicate our public messages,” she said.
Ms Fu said the daily PSI forecast helps the public plan activities for the next day, while hourly PM2.5 readings can guide immediate outdoor activities.
